etymologies.etymologyHTML:
Preposition and adverb from Middle English aboute, abouten, from Old English abūtan, onbūtan, from on (“in, on”) +‎ būtan (“outside of”), itself from be (“by”) +‎ ūtan (“outside”). Cognate with Old Frisian abûta (“outside; except”).

Adjective from Middle English about (adverb).

definitions.definition: In a circle around; all round; on every side of; on the outside of. [from before 1150][2]

definitions.definition: (with 'to' and verb infinitive) See about to.
(with present participle, obsolete or dialect) On the point or verge of.

definitions.definition: Indicates that something will happen very soon; indicates a plan or intention to do something.

Improving the workings of the businesses they take over is just as core to their calling, if not more so. Much of their pleading is public-relations bluster.

He drew away her hands from her face, when she said gently, "Have you much money about you?" / "Oh the mercenary baggage!" said the traveller to himself; and then replied aloud, "Why, pretty one?—Do you sell your kisses so high, then?"

definitions.definition: (figurative) In or near, as in mental faculties or (literally) in the possession of; under the control of; at one's command; in one's makeup. [from ca. 1350–1470][2]

definitions.definition: Near; in the vicinity. [from ca. 1350–1470[2]]
(nautical) To the opposite tack: see go about. [from late 15th c.[2]]
